# Reflexes and Safety Enforcement\chaptersubtitle{System 1 1000 Hz Control Barrier Functions, Compliance, and Motor FOC} {#sec-enforcement}

![**Systems Organ Focus:** Stage 6 (Real-Time Reflex and 1 kHz Safety Enforcement). Operating on a dedicated bare-metal microcontroller in zero-allocation static SRAM (`malloc = 0`), this stage evaluates Control Barrier Functions ($h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$) at $1000\text{ Hz}$ to minimally project candidate neural actions onto safe half-spaces before commanding $20\text{ kHz}$ motor gate drivers.](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch09 fig-pos="H" width=100%}

*Why does a software safety guardrail written in Python fail to stop a robot from injuring a human during an OS memory compaction pause?*

In cloud software systems, safety guardrails are implemented as application-level middleware filters, assertion checks, or wrapper scripts. In Physical AI, software safety checks co-located on a general-purpose operating system share the same execution thread, memory bus, and scheduling vulnerability as the neural models they are meant to supervise. When the host operating system experiences a memory compaction stall, thread preemption, or runtime crash, unmanaged motor registers remain latched and moving mass crashes into the environment. Physical AI resolves this vulnerability through the Proposal–Permission Privilege Split: high-capacity neural models propose actions from an untrusted Linux domain, while a dedicated, bare-metal microcontroller executing in zero-allocation static SRAM holds exclusive electrical authority to evaluate Control Barrier Functions and veto hazardous commands in sub-millisecond real time.


{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-objective}
After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

1. **Implement Zero-Allocation 1000 Hz MCU Enforcers:** Construct hard real-time safety filters on dedicated ARM Cortex-M7 and lockstep RISC-V microcontroller silicon with bounded worst-case execution latency ($\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$) and zero dynamic heap allocation (`malloc = 0`).
2. **Formulate Control Barrier Functions (CBFs):** Formulate continuously differentiable barrier certificates $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$ guaranteeing the forward invariance of safe operating sets $\mathcal{C}$ under non-linear control-affine dynamics.
3. **Solve Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Programs (CBF-QPs):** Project unverified candidate action proposals ($\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$) emitted by neural policies onto admissible safety half-spaces ($\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}$) using active-set solvers in static SRAM.
4. **Enforce Dynamic Stopping Envelopes ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clearance}}$):** Intercept and veto trajectory proposals that violate clearance margins relative to stationary and moving obstacles before physical contact occurs.
5. **Implement Contact Impedance and Passivity Control:** Formulate virtual spring-damper compliance ($\mathbf{M}_d, \mathbf{D}_d, \mathbf{K}_d$) and passivity energy tanks to stabilize physical contact interactions without kinematic singularities.
6. **Command Motor Field-Oriented Control (FOC):** Direct $20\text{ kHz}$ Space-Vector Pulse-Width Modulation (SVPWM) switching via Clarke and Park transforms in dedicated hardware timer peripherals.
7. **Dissect OS Latency Blowout Collisions:** Analyze the Late Commanded Deceleration autopsy where a $140\text{ ms}$ Linux dirty page writeback stall caused a $3.4\text{ kN}$ collision that fractured a harmonic drive flexspline.
8. **Freeze the Safety Enforcement Interface:** Author the formal engineering specification establishing 1000 Hz timer schedules, CBF parameters, the IEC 60204-1 emergency stop hierarchy, and hardware Safe Torque Off optocoupler lines.

**Core Chapter Takeaway:** Physical safety cannot be delegated to application software or learned neural policies; it requires a dedicated bare-metal System 1 permission authority operating at $1000\text{ Hz}$ in zero-allocation static SRAM (`malloc = 0`) that solves Control Barrier Function Quadratic Programs (CBF-QPs) to minimally perturb candidate actions and guarantee forward set invariance.
:::


## Real-Time Safety Enforcement

In @sec-planning, we engineered the System 1.5 trajectory planning organ, which generates continuous, multi-step action chunks ($H=16$) to bridge the cadence gap between high-level semantic reasoning ($1\text{ Hz}$) and low-level actuator control (@fig-locator-ch09). However, passing these generative trajectories directly to physical motor drives introduces a lethal vulnerability. In conventional robotics stacks, motion planning, trajectory synthesis, and safety monitoring are frequently bundled into a monolithic application process executing under a standard operating system. In modern Physical AI architectures, where high-level reasoning and trajectory synthesis are driven by multi-billion parameter foundation models and diffusion decoders, this monolithic design is fatal.

### The Physical Analogy: Hydraulic Brake Assist and the Silicon Shield

To understand why software-only safety fails, consider a tangible physical mental model: **The Hydraulic Brake Assist Overriding the Electronic Accelerator**. In a modern drive-by-wire automobile, the driver or autonomous cruise-control computer may depress the electronic throttle pedal, requesting full engine acceleration. However, a dedicated hydraulic anti-lock braking system (ABS) module—hardwired directly to wheel-speed sensors and hydraulic brake calipers—holds physical override authority. The instant millimeter-wave radar detects a stopped obstacle within the physical stopping distance, the hydraulic ABS valves pulse fluid pressure into the calipers, arresting the vehicle's momentum regardless of the electronic throttle command. The software throttle *proposes*, but the physical hydraulic circuit holds absolute *permission* authority.

In Physical AI, we implement this exact separation across heterogeneous silicon:

A general-purpose operating system such as standard Linux is engineered to optimize average throughput across competing processes. In doing so, it routinely introduces non-deterministic latency spikes: kernel memory compaction pauses, dirty page background flushes, thread preemption, and bus contention across shared DRAM crossbars (@fig-enforcer-timing). If safety monitoring resides in user-space software on the Linux host, any operating system stall halts the safety monitor simultaneously with the neural policy. During that stall, unserviced motor command registers remain latched while moving mass continues to coast forward under unguided momentum ($d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t$). For a robotic manipulator traveling at an operational velocity of $v = 1.5\text{ m/s}$, a modest $140\text{ ms}$ Linux kernel memory compaction stall results in $d_{\text{coast}} = 210\text{ mm}$ ($21\text{ cm}$) of completely unmonitored displacement, converting software scheduling jitter directly into a destructive physical collision.

![**System 1 Microsecond Timer Waterfall and Proposal-Permission Boundary.** Dedicated bare-metal MCU executes a strict $1000\text{ Hz}$ ($1.0\text{ ms} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$) timer interrupt. Ingesting candidate spline waypoints from shared SRAM mailboxes, reading $1000\text{ Hz}$ joint telemetry, solving the Minimal-Intervention CBF-QP in $< 175\,\mu\text{s}$, and writing Space-Vector PWM registers to drive motor inverters.](figures/fig08_enforcer_timing_waterfall.svg){#fig-enforcer-timing width=100%}

### The Proposal–Permission Privilege Split

Physical AI resolves this vulnerability through the **Proposal–Permission Privilege Split**. The system is partitioned across heterogeneous silicon into two isolated operational domains (@tbl-proposal-permission-ch09):

The untrusted proposal domain encompasses large Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and generative trajectory decoders (ACT, Diffusion Policies) executing on multi-core Linux Application Processors (MPUs) and edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs). This domain possesses rich semantic intelligence and wide receptive fields but is treated from a safety standpoint as an untrusted proposal service. It generates candidate trajectory chunks accompanied by expiring intent leases ($\tau_{\text{lease}} \approx 50\text{--}100\text{ ms}$), depositing them into lock-free shared memory mailboxes.

The sole hardware permission authority belongs to a dedicated, hard real-time microcontroller (such as an ARM Cortex-M7 or dual-core lockstep RISC-V) executing bare-metal or on a microsecond RTOS kernel in tightly coupled static SRAM. This microcontroller possesses exclusive physical routing to the gate drivers of the motor inverters. It evaluates candidate trajectory chunks against non-negotiable physical invariants at a deterministic $1000\text{ Hz}$ ($1.0\text{ ms} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$) cadence. If an intent lease expires without renewal due to an upstream operating system stall, the microcontroller automatically clamps acceleration and executes a safe controlled stop.

| System Dimension | Untrusted Proposal Domain (System 2 / 1.5) | Bare-Metal Permission Authority (System 1) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Compute Silicon** | Multi-core Host MPU (ARM Cortex-A78, x86-64) & Edge NPU | Dedicated Real-Time MCU (ARM Cortex-M7, Lockstep RISC-V) |
| **Operating System** | General-purpose Linux with dynamic memory management | Bare-metal firmware / Microsecond RTOS (`malloc = 0`) |
| **Memory Discipline** | Virtual memory with DRAM paging, caching, and GC | Zero-allocation static DTCM SRAM with compile-time bounds |
| **Execution Cadence** | Asynchronous $1\text{--}20\text{ Hz}$ with $P_{99} > 100\text{ ms}$ tails | Deterministic $1000\text{ Hz}$ timer ISR ($1.0\text{ ms} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$) |
| **Algorithmic Role** | Semantic reasoning, scene understanding, spline proposals | CBF-QP projection, stopping invariants, 20 kHz FOC inverters |
| **Hardware Authority** | Zero direct electrical connection to motor gate inverters | Exclusive physical routing to gate driver PWM and STO lines |

: Proposal–Permission Privilege Split. Heterogeneous silicon separation between untrusted generative AI proposals and hard real-time safety enforcement. {#tbl-proposal-permission-ch09}

Microcontroller firmware strictly obeys the iron law of deterministic execution (`malloc = 0`): zero dynamic heap allocations, zero blocking mutexes, and zero reliance on operating system threads. Every matrix, buffer, and data structure is allocated statically at compile time. By bounding the worst-case execution time to $\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$, the safety enforcer guarantees that invariants are evaluated with microsecond precision, ensuring the physical survival of the machine even if the host Linux operating system crashes or freezes.

Mastering this real-time safety enforcement layer requires bridging three engineering perspectives:

- **Maya (CS/ML):** Trains high-capacity foundation models and diffusion decoders that generate trajectory chunks in Python and PyTorch, while learning why soft reward penalties ($\mathbb{E}[R] - \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{penalty}}$) fail to guarantee zero boundary violations in out-of-distribution corner cases.
- **Carlos (ECE/Embedded):** Architects the bare-metal System 1 enforcer in static DTCM SRAM (`malloc = 0`), structuring $1000\text{ Hz} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$ timer ISRs, lock-free SRAM mailboxes, and hardware Safe Torque Off optocoupler interlocks.
- **Alex (MechE/Robotics):** Grounds barrier certificates in physical kinematics, second-order stopping distances ($d_{\text{stop}} = v \tau_{\text{latency}} + v^2 / 2a_{\text{max}}$), Cartesian impedance compliance ($\mathbf{M}_d, \mathbf{D}_d, \mathbf{K}_d$), and back-EMF torque saturation to protect mechanical gearboxes from stress fracture.

The architecture begins by establishing Control Barrier Functions to guarantee mathematical forward set invariance (Section 9.2), transforming physical safety boundaries into linear constraints on motor inputs that act as a speed governor as clearance decreases. To execute these invariants on real hardware, the microcontroller solves a Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Program at every millisecond tick (Section 9.3), passing safe AI proposals untouched and computing minimal projections when danger threatens. The physical reflex layer couples this mathematical shield with dynamic stopping distance bounds, Cartesian impedance control, passivity energy tanks, and 20 kHz Field-Oriented Control (Section 9.4), grounding digital decisions in the physical realities of friction cones, contact forces, and motor thermal dissipation. When upstream software or hardware fails, the system executes a certified multi-tier escalation hierarchy from trajectory freeze down to hardware-isolated Safe Torque Off (Section 9.5). Finally, we examine the forensic autopsy of an industrial gearbox fracture caused by an operating system latency tail, compile the formal safety enforcement specification, expose pervasive safety fallacies, and synthesize the five sensory-motor organs that conclude Part II.


## Control Barrier Functions

In empirical machine learning, researchers frequently attempt to enforce safety by adding penalty terms to a reward function during reinforcement learning or by adding loss penalties during behavioral cloning. For **Maya (CS/ML)**, who is accustomed to shaping objective functions in simulator training runs, this seems like the natural approach. On physical hardware, however, soft loss penalties are fundamentally inadequate: they merely alter statistical expectations ($\mathbb{E}[R]$), readily permitting low-probability, catastrophic constraint violations when the system encounters novel out-of-distribution inputs. When an unmodeled optical glare or novel obstacle geometry induces an unfamiliar input state, a neural policy that scored $99.9\%$ in simulation can still command full voltage into a rigid barrier.

### The Physical Analogy: The Invisible Magnetic Repelling Cushion

To build physical intuition for Control Barrier Functions, consider the mental model of an **Invisible Magnetic Repelling Cushion and Dynamic Speed Governor**. Imagine surrounding the robot and all environmental obstacles with a specialized magnetic force field. 

When the robot maneuvers deep within the safe open workspace ($h(\mathbf{x}) \gg 0$), the magnetic field is completely dormant: it exerts zero drag or resistance, allowing the machine to track learned trajectories at maximum operational speed with full behavioral dexterity. However, as the robot approaches a physical boundary ($h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0$), the repelling field activates smoothly. Rather than acting as a rigid brick wall that causes a sudden, high-jerk deceleration, the field acts as an adaptive speed governor: it throttles the maximum allowable approach speed in direct linear proportion to remaining physical clearance. As clearance shrinks to zero ($h(\mathbf{x}) = 0$), the maximum allowable approach velocity is smoothly clamped to exactly zero ($\dot{h} \ge 0$), rendering the safety boundary physically impenetrable.

### The Mathematics of Forward Set Invariance

We now formulate this invariant using our four-step pedagogical structure:

1. **Physical Hazard:** When an embodied agent moves under continuous physics, momentum prevents instantaneous changes in velocity. If safety is evaluated only at the boundary ($h(\mathbf{x}) = 0$), moving mass will inevitably breach the perimeter due to actuator saturation and finite braking capacity. Safety must be enforced dynamically throughout the interior of the safe set by constraining the time rate of change of clearance ($\dot{h}(\mathbf{x})$).
2. **Mathematical Formulation:** Consider a continuous non-linear control-affine dynamical system:
   $$\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}$$
   where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ represents the physical state vector, $\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U} \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ is the control input, $f(\mathbf{x})$ describes autonomous drift dynamics, and $g(\mathbf{x})$ defines the input mapping.

   We define the admissible safe operating set $\mathcal{C} \subset \mathcal{X}$ as the 0-superlevel set of a continuously differentiable scalar barrier certificate function $h: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$:
   $$\mathcal{C} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \;\middle|\; h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \right\}$$
   $$\partial \mathcal{C} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \;\middle|\; h(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \right\} \quad (\text{Safe Boundary})$$
   $$\text{Int}(\mathcal{C}) = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \;\middle|\; h(\mathbf{x}) > 0 \right\} \quad (\text{Interior Safe Region})$$

   The safe set $\mathcal{C}$ is **forward invariant** if for every initial state starting within the set ($\mathbf{x}(0) \in \mathcal{C}$), the trajectory remains strictly inside the set for all future time ($\mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathcal{C}, \forall t \ge 0$). By Nagumo's Invariance Theorem [@ames2014control; @ames2019control], forward set invariance is guaranteed if and only if the control input $\mathbf{u}$ satisfies the fundamental Control Barrier Function (CBF) inequality:
   $$\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}) \ge -\gamma h(\mathbf{x}) \iff L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \gamma h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$$

3. **Variable and Intuition Breakdown:**
   - $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the physical state (e.g., joint angles in $\text{rad}$, velocities in $\text{rad/s}$, end-effector coordinates in $\text{m}$).
   - $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is the commanded actuator input (e.g., motor torques in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ or phase currents in $\text{A}$).
   - $h(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the scalar barrier certificate representing the instantaneous safety margin (such as geometric clearance $d - r_{\text{safe}}$ or thermal headroom $T_{\text{max}} - T_{\text{stator}}$).
   - $\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}$ is the row-vector spatial gradient of the barrier function with respect to the state.
   - $L_f h(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) f(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}$ is the **Lie derivative** of $h$ along the autonomous drift dynamics $f$, measuring the unforced time rate of change of the safety margin under gravity, velocity, and friction.
   - $L_g h(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) g(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times m}$ is the **Lie derivative** of $h$ along the control vector field $g$, representing the instantaneous directional control authority available to modulate the barrier via actuator inputs $\mathbf{u}$.
   - $\gamma > 0$ is a positive linear convergence gain with physical units of $\text{s}^{-1}$, functioning as the speed governor sensitivity.

4. **Concrete Numerical Walkthroughs Across Archetypes:**

   - **Archetype 1: Mobility (Obstacle Clearance Barrier):** For an autonomous mobile robot navigating in 2D space with Cartesian position $\mathbf{p} = [p_x, p_y]^T \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and obstacle location $\mathbf{p}_{\text{obs}} \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the safety margin is defined relative to the certified clearance radius $r_{\text{safe}} = 0.50\text{ m}$:
     $$h_{\text{obs}}(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{obs}}\|^2 - r_{\text{safe}}^2 \ge 0$$
     Differentiating along kinematics $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{v}$ yields the linear velocity constraint:
     $$2(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{obs}})^T \mathbf{v} \ge -\gamma_{\text{obs}} \left( \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{obs}}\|^2 - r_{\text{safe}}^2 \right)$$

     *Numerical Evaluation:* Position the mobile robot at $\mathbf{p} = [1.50, 0.00]^T\text{ m}$ heading toward an obstacle at the origin $\mathbf{p}_{\text{obs}} = [0.00, 0.00]^T\text{ m}$ with governor gain $\gamma_{\text{obs}} = 2.0\text{ s}^{-1}$.

     - At $\mathbf{p} = [1.50, 0.00]^T\text{ m}$, barrier value is $h = 1.50^2 - 0.50^2 = 2.25 - 0.25 = 2.00\text{ m}^2$. The barrier inequality enforces:
       $$2 [1.50, 0.00] \begin{bmatrix} v_x \\ v_y \end{bmatrix} \ge -2.0(2.00) \implies 3.00 v_x \ge -4.00 \implies v_x \ge -1.33\text{ m/s}$$
       The robot is permitted to approach the obstacle at up to $1.33\text{ m/s}$.

     - When the robot advances to $\mathbf{p} = [0.60, 0.00]^T\text{ m}$ (only $10\text{ cm}$ of clearance outside $r_{\text{safe}}$), the barrier contracts to $h = 0.60^2 - 0.50^2 = 0.36 - 0.25 = 0.11\text{ m}^2$. The velocity constraint tightens automatically to:
       $$2(0.60) v_x \ge -2.0(0.11) \implies 1.20 v_x \ge -0.22 \implies v_x \ge -0.183\text{ m/s}$$
       The barrier automatically throttles maximum allowable approach speed from $1.33\text{ m/s}$ down to $0.183\text{ m/s}$, smoothly reaching $0.00\text{ m/s}$ at $r_{\text{safe}} = 0.50\text{ m}$.

   - **Archetype 2: Contact Manipulation (Joint Limit and Kinematic Braking Barrier):** For an articulated robot arm governed by joint angles $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the barrier incorporates Torricelli's kinematic braking envelope ($v^2 = 2 a \Delta x$) to prevent hard-stop collisions:
     $$h_{\text{joint}}(q_i, \dot{q}_i) = 2 \ddot{q}_{\text{max}, i} (q_i - q_{\text{min}, i}) - \dot{q}_i^2 \ge 0 \quad (\text{for approach to lower stop } q_{\text{min}, i} \text{ with } \dot{q}_i < 0)$$

     *Numerical Evaluation:* A manipulator wrist joint approaches its lower travel limit $q_{\text{min}} = -1.50\text{ rad}$ from current position $q = -1.30\text{ rad}$ (remaining travel $\Delta q = 0.20\text{ rad}$) with maximum certified braking deceleration $\ddot{q}_{\text{max}} = 10.0\text{ rad/s}^2$. The barrier evaluates to:
     $$h_{\text{joint}} = 2(10.0)(0.20) - \dot{q}^2 = 4.00 - \dot{q}^2 \ge 0 \implies |\dot{q}| \le \sqrt{4.00} = 2.00\text{ rad/s}$$
     If an unverified neural policy commands a joint velocity of $\dot{q}_{\text{cand}} = -2.50\text{ rad/s}$, the barrier evaluates to $h = 4.00 - 6.25 = -2.25 < 0$ (unsafe). The safety enforcer immediately clamps the joint velocity to $-2.00\text{ rad/s}$, ensuring that the joint can decelerate to a complete stop before striking the physical mechanical hard stop.

   - **Archetype 3: Cybernetics (Actuator Thermal and Current Protection Barrier):** For high-bandwidth motor drives, the barrier prevents stator coil insulation breakdown ($155^\circ\text{C}$ NEMA Class F):
     $$h_{\text{thermal}}(T_{\text{stator}}) = T_{\text{max}} - T_{\text{stator}} \ge 0$$
     The stator temperature evolves according to the continuous thermal differential equation:
     $$\dot{T}_{\text{stator}} = \frac{1}{C_{\text{th}}} \left( I_{\text{rms}}^2 R_{\text{stator}} - \frac{T_{\text{stator}} - T_{\text{amb}}}{R_{\text{th}}} \right)$$
     *Numerical Evaluation:* Consider a motor with winding resistance $R_{\text{stator}} = 0.25\,\Omega$, thermal capacitance $C_{\text{th}} = 60.0\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$, thermal resistance $R_{\text{th}} = 2.00^\circ\text{C/W}$, ambient temperature $T_{\text{amb}} = 25.0^\circ\text{C}$, maximum rating $T_{\text{max}} = 100.0^\circ\text{C}$, and gain $\gamma_{\text{th}} = 0.20\text{ s}^{-1}$.
     When the stator reaches $T_{\text{stator}} = 85.0^\circ\text{C}$ ($15.0^\circ\text{C}$ of headroom remaining), the barrier inequality $-\dot{T}_{\text{stator}} \ge -\gamma_{\text{th}}(T_{\text{max}} - T_{\text{stator}})$ enforces:
     $$\dot{T}_{\text{stator}} \le 0.20(100.0 - 85.0) = 0.20(15.0) = 3.00^\circ\text{C/s}$$
     The convective heat loss is $\frac{85.0 - 25.0}{2.00} = 30.0\text{ W}$. Substituting into the thermal model yields:
     $$\frac{1}{60.0} \left( I^2(0.25) - 30.0 \right) \le 3.00 \implies I^2(0.25) \le 210.0\text{ W} \implies I \le \sqrt{840.0} = 28.98\text{ A}$$
     The safety enforcer directly translates thermal headroom into a hard upper bound on allowable phase current ($I \le 29.0\text{ A}$), linearly derating motor torque before enamel insulation is permanently compromised.

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Global Forward Invariance vs. Local QP Myopia and Relative Degree Deadlock"}
* **The Common Assumption:** A valid mathematical Control Barrier Function $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$ satisfying $L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \gamma h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$ guarantees that the robot will remain forward invariant within the safe set $\mathcal{C}$ under all operating conditions and arbitrary candidate control inputs.
* **The Physical Reality:** A standard Control Barrier Function evaluated point-wise inside a 1 kHz Quadratic Program operates myopically in time. In physical systems, position constraints have relative degree 2 with respect to commanded motor torques ($\mathbf{u}$). When a heavy mechanical arm approaches a boundary at high velocity, the local QP solver may find valid instantaneous solutions that satisfy $\dot{h} \ge -\gamma h$ at step $k$, but drive the state into an *inescapable set*—a region where the required deceleration at step $k+1$ exceeds the physical torque or current saturation limits of the motor inverters ($|\mathbf{u}| > \mathbf{u}_{\text{max}}$). The QP solver suddenly encounters primal infeasibility ($\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}} = \emptyset$), leaving the enforcer with no admissible mathematical control command and causing an uncommanded boundary breach.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Safety certificates for second-order dynamical systems must employ High-Order or Exponential Control Barrier Functions (ECBFs) that explicitly account for state-dependent braking dynamics, coupled with viability kernel analysis that constrains the admissible boundary $\partial \mathcal{C}$ to states where certified braking deceleration $a_{\text{max}}$ remains strictly feasible under actuator saturation limits $\mathbf{u} \in [\mathbf{u}_{\text{min}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{max}}]$.
:::


## Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Programs

To merge unverified candidate action proposals from generative neural models ($\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$) with hard physical safety guarantees, the System 1 microcontroller solves a Minimal-Intervention Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (CBF-QP) at every $1000\text{ Hz}$ control cycle (@fig-cbf-projection).

![**Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Programming Projection.** The unverified candidate action $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ generated by the neural policy is projected onto the admissible half-space $\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}$ defined by active Control Barrier Function hyperplanes. When the proposal is safe, it passes unmodified ($\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$); when it threatens a barrier breach, the QP minimally alters the command to ensure forward invariance.](figures/fig08_cbf_projection.svg){#fig-cbf-projection width=100%}

### The Physical Analogy: The Elastic Safety Leash and Minimal Projection

To understand the role of the safety filter, consider the mental model of an **Elastic Safety Leash and Minimal-Projection Shield**. When walking an agile, energetic dog, a loose leash allows the animal complete freedom to explore, run, and choose its path. As long as the dog remains on the safe sidewalk, the leash remains completely slack: you exert zero force, preserving $100\%$ of the animal's natural gait and intent. 

However, the instant the dog dashes toward the edge of the street, the leash pulls taut at the boundary. Crucially, you do not yank the dog entirely back to the starting line or freeze its legs; you exert only the exact directional tension needed to keep its paws on the sidewalk perimeter.

In Physical AI, the Minimal-Intervention QP acts as this exact elastic leash for generative neural policies:

- **Unconstrained Flow:** As long as the candidate action $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ emitted by the neural model satisfies all barrier certificates ($L_f h_i + L_g h_i \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} + \gamma_i h_i \ge 0$), the safety filter is completely passive. The command passes through untouched ($\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$) in zero solver iterations, preserving the policy's rich behavioral dexterity.
- **Minimal Projection:** When a candidate action threatens to breach a barrier (such as commanding excessive acceleration toward a wall or over-current into a motor), the corresponding barrier hyperplane activates. The QP calculates the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ onto the boundary of the safe half-space $\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}$, modifying the neural command only by the absolute mathematical minimum needed to guarantee forward set invariance.

### The Mathematics of Active-Set Quadratic Programming

We formulate the minimal-intervention optimization using our four-step pedagogical structure:

1. **Physical Hazard:** Overriding a learned neural policy with coarse heuristic emergency stops (such as zeroing all motor torques or slamming mechanical brakes) disrupts smooth task execution, induces extreme structural jerk, and destroys policy dexterity. The safety filter must minimally alter candidate commands only along the specific spatial directions that threaten barrier violation.
2. **Mathematical Formulation:** The minimal-intervention problem is formulated as a convex Quadratic Program:
   $$\mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m} \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \right)^T \mathbf{W} \left( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \right)$$
   $$\begin{aligned}
   \text{subject to} \quad &L_f h_i(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \gamma_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0, \quad i = 1, \dots, M_{\text{barriers}} \\
   &\mathbf{u}_{\text{min}} \le \mathbf{u} \le \mathbf{u}_{\text{max}} \quad (\text{Actuator Saturation Limits})
   \end{aligned}$$

   When one or more barriers are violated ($L_f h_i + L_g h_i \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} + \gamma_i h_i < 0$), the active-set solver identifies the active constraint subset $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \{1, \dots, M_{\text{barriers}}\}$ and solves the equality-constrained Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) linear system:
   $$\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{W} & -\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T \\ \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{u}^* \\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^* \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{W}\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \\ \mathbf{b}_{\mathcal{A}} \end{bmatrix}$$

   Solving via the Schur complement yields the exact analytical projected command:
   $$\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} - \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T \left( \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T \right)^{-1} \left( \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} - \mathbf{b}_{\mathcal{A}} \right)$$
   $$\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^* = \left( \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T \right)^{-1} \left( \mathbf{b}_{\mathcal{A}} - \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \right)$$

3. **Variable and Intuition Breakdown:**
   - $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is the unverified candidate actuator command proposed by the neural policy (e.g., joint torques in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ or phase currents in $\text{A}$).
   - $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$ is a symmetric positive-definite weighting metric, prioritizing which actuator channels can be altered (e.g., heavily penalizing changes to gripper orientation while permitting base adjustments).
   - $\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} = [ L_g h_i(\mathbf{x}) ]_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}| \times m}$ is the matrix of stacked active barrier gradients.
   - $\mathbf{b}_{\mathcal{A}} = [ -L_f h_i(\mathbf{x}) - \gamma_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) ]_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|}$ is the active boundary vector.
   - $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^* \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|}$ is the vector of non-negative Lagrange multipliers ($\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^* \ge 0$), representing the physical "tension" or marginal cost of enforcing each active safety constraint.

4. **Concrete Numerical Walkthrough:**
   Consider a 2-joint planar robotic arm ($m = 2$) receiving a candidate torque command $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} = [4.00, 2.00]^T\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ with uniform weighting $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}_2$. A single obstacle barrier constraint ($|\mathcal{A}| = 1$) is active, parameterized by gradient $\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} = [1.0, 2.0]$ and threshold $b_{\mathcal{A}} = 10.00\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ (enforcing $1.0 u_1 + 2.0 u_2 \ge 10.00$).

   - *Step 1: Evaluate candidate against barrier:*
     $$\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} = 1.0(4.00) + 2.0(2.00) = 4.00 + 4.00 = 8.00\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$$
     Because $8.00 < 10.00$, the neural proposal breaches the safety margin by a deficit of $2.00\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

   - *Step 2: Compute Gramian scalar:*
     $$\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T = [1.0, 2.0] \begin{bmatrix} 1.0 \\ 2.0 \end{bmatrix} = 1.0^2 + 2.0^2 = 5.00$$

   - *Step 3: Calculate projected torque command:*
     $$\mathbf{u}^* = \begin{bmatrix} 4.00 \\ 2.00 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1.0 \\ 2.0 \end{bmatrix} \left( \frac{1}{5.00} \right) (8.00 - 10.00) = \begin{bmatrix} 4.00 \\ 2.00 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0.40 \\ 0.80 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4.40 \\ 2.80 \end{bmatrix}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$$

   - *Step 4: Verify boundary satisfaction and minimum deviation:*
     $$1.0(4.40) + 2.0(2.80) = 4.40 + 5.60 = 10.00\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$$
     $$\lambda^* = \frac{10.00 - 8.00}{5.00} = 0.40 \ge 0$$
     The projected command satisfies the safety barrier exactly on the boundary, deviating from the candidate proposal by the absolute minimum squared Euclidean distance of $\|\mathbf{u}^* - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}\|^2 = 0.40^2 + 0.80^2 = 0.80\text{ (N}\cdot\text{m)}^2$.

### Zero-Allocation Embedded Execution on ARM Cortex-M7

Because this optimization must complete in $\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$ inside an embedded microcontroller, the firmware employs pre-compiled, statically allocated active-set solvers. On embedded silicon, computing matrix inversions at runtime with dynamic memory allocation is prohibitive. The firmware pre-allocates static factorization buffers ($L D L^T$ or Cholesky) in Tightly Coupled Memory (DTCM SRAM) for a maximum active set dimension $|\mathcal{A}| \le m$. The active-set iterations update the factorization via rank-one Givens rotations, guaranteeing deterministic convergence in bounded clock cycles.

Operating in DTCM SRAM with zero dynamic memory allocation (`malloc = 0`), an ARM Cortex-M7 running at $480\text{ MHz}$ solves a 6-DoF CBF-QP in fewer than $84{,}000$ clock cycles, consuming less than $8\text{ KB}$ of static memory. This guarantees that even during worst-case active-set iterations, execution consumes only $17.5\%$ of the $1000\,\mu\text{s}$ timer interrupt window, leaving ample headroom for sensor telemetry ingestion and inverter modulation. Complete multi-variable KKT matrix expansions and the full embedded C active-set solver implementation are provided in Appendix Section 3.

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Dynamic Heap Allocation and General-Purpose Solvers on Microcontroller Silicon"}
* **The Common Assumption:** Standard open-source interior-point and ADMM convex optimization libraries provide robust, production-grade QP solving that can be dropped directly into an embedded microcontroller safety loop.
* **The Physical Reality:** General-purpose solvers rely on dynamic heap allocation (`malloc`, `free`, `realloc`) during matrix factorization, line searches, and constraint updates. In a 1 kHz bare-metal ISR, heap allocation causes memory fragmentation and risks heap exhaustion crashes. Crucially, interior-point algorithms exhibit non-deterministic iteration counts, with execution times fluctuating wildly from $40\,\mu\text{s}$ under nominal conditions to $>2500\,\mu\text{s}$ near ill-conditioned constraint boundaries. If a 1 kHz timer interrupt takes $2.5\text{ ms}$ to solve a safety QP, it overruns the control deadline, causing actuator watchdog trips or uncommanded motor shutdown.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Embedded safety filters executing inside hard real-time interrupt routines must enforce strict zero-allocation memory discipline (`malloc = 0`). Solvers must be statically pre-allocated active-set or dual-projected gradient methods with mathematically bounded maximum iteration counts, guaranteeing worst-case execution time $\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$ in static DTCM SRAM.
:::


## Stopping Envelopes and Impedance Control

Safety enforcement on physical hardware requires grounding digital optimization in the physical dynamics of moving mass, contact mechanics, and electromagnetic torque generation.

### Dynamic Stopping Clearance and Reaction Drift

At every millisecond tick, the microcontroller monitors physical clearance relative to obstacles. In physical reality, moving mass cannot stop instantaneously: arresting kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$) requires mechanical work done by opposing braking forces ($W = \int \mathbf{F}_{\text{brake}} \cdot d\mathbf{x}$) over finite distance and time.

We formulate the dynamic stopping invariant using our four-step pedagogical structure:

1. **Physical Hazard:** When an embodied agent detects an obstacle, moving mass continues coasting during computational deliberation and sensor transmission before braking forces can ramp up. If the enforcer sizes clearance only for kinematic braking without accounting for transport latency, this reaction drift will cause high-speed kinetic impacts.
2. **Mathematical Formulation:** The total dynamic stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}}(v)$ is the sum of reaction drift displacement and quadratic kinematic braking distance:
   $$d_{\text{stop}}(v) = \underbrace{v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}}}_{\text{Reaction Drift}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}}_{\text{Kinematic Braking}}$$

   The fundamental safety invariant evaluated at $1000\text{ Hz}$ requires that measured clearance $d_{\text{clearance}}(\mathbf{x})$ strictly exceed dynamic stopping distance plus a certified safety buffer $d_{\text{margin}}$:
   $$d_{\text{clearance}}(\mathbf{x}) \ge d_{\text{stop}}(v) + d_{\text{margin}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}} + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}} + d_{\text{margin}}$$

   When a proposed trajectory commands a velocity $v_{\text{cand}}$ that violates this inequality, the microcontroller clamps the setpoint to the exact parabolic braking envelope $v_{\text{safe}}$:
   $$v_{\text{safe}} = \sqrt{a_{\text{max}}^2 \tau_{\text{latency}}^2 + 2 a_{\text{max}} \left( d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{margin}} \right)} - a_{\text{max}} \tau_{\text{latency}}$$

3. **Variable and Intuition Breakdown:**
   - $v = \|\dot{\mathbf{x}}\|$ is the instantaneous operational velocity in meters per second ($\text{m/s}$).
   - $\tau_{\text{latency}}$ is the total worst-case hardware sensorimotor latency (including camera exposure, bus serialization, and inverter filter lag, typically $12.0\text{ ms}$).
   - $a_{\text{max}}$ is the certified maximum braking deceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$, constrained by Coulomb friction, payload stability, or motor torque saturation.
   - $d_{\text{clearance}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the measured physical distance to the nearest obstacle in meters ($\text{m}$).
   - $d_{\text{margin}}$ is the certified minimum safety buffer in meters ($\text{m}$, typically $0.020\text{ m} = 20\text{ mm}$).

4. **Concrete Numerical Walkthrough:**
   Consider a manipulator traveling at $v_{\text{cand}} = 1.50\text{ m/s}$ with transport latency $\tau_{\text{latency}} = 12.0\text{ ms}$ ($0.012\text{ s}$), maximum certified braking deceleration $a_{\text{max}} = 4.0\text{ m/s}^2$, and safety margin $d_{\text{margin}} = 0.020\text{ m}$. If a sensor detects an obstacle at $d_{\text{clearance}} = 0.150\text{ m}$ ($15\text{ cm}$):

   - *Candidate stopping requirement:*
     $$d_{\text{stop}}(1.50) + d_{\text{margin}} = (1.50 \times 0.012) + \frac{1.50^2}{2 \times 4.0} + 0.020 = 0.018 + 0.281 + 0.020 = 0.319\text{ m}$$
     Because $0.319\text{ m} > 0.150\text{ m}$, the proposal would cause a destructive collision.

   - *Microcontroller speed clamp (evaluated in $< 5\,\mu\text{s}$):*
     $$v_{\text{safe}} = \sqrt{(4.0 \times 0.012)^2 + 2(4.0)(0.150 - 0.020)} - (4.0 \times 0.012) = \sqrt{0.0023 + 1.040} - 0.048 = 0.973\text{ m/s}$$
     The microcontroller instantly clamps the velocity setpoint from $1.50\text{ m/s}$ down to $0.973\text{ m/s}$, containing kinetic energy within the physical braking boundary.

### Contact Impedance Control and Passivity Energy Tanks

While rigid position control is effective for free-space motion, it is hazardous during physical contact manipulation and locomotion foot placement. When a manipulator interacts with a rigid surface (such as inserting a component, polishing a workpiece, or contacting an operator), small calibration errors generate extreme contact force spikes:
$$F_{\text{contact}} = k_{\text{env}} \cdot \Delta x$$

Because the stiffness of steel or aluminum fixtures exceeds $k_{\text{env}} > 10^6\text{ N/m}$, a positional tracking error of just $0.5\text{ mm}$ produces contact forces exceeding $500\text{ N}$, stalling motors and damaging precision gear teeth.

#### The Physical Analogy: The Programmable Mechanical Shock Absorber {.unnumbered}

To prevent catastrophic contact forces, consider the mental model of a **Programmable Mechanical Shock Absorber**. Instead of acting as an unyielding granite wall, the robot's end-effector is rendered electronically as a compliant mass-spring-damper system. When external forces push against the robot, the joint torques yield smoothly like a soft mechanical spring, absorbing kinetic energy and cushioning the interaction.

#### The Mathematics of Impedance and Stiffness Control {.unnumbered}

We formulate contact compliance using our four-step pedagogical structure:

1. **Physical Hazard:** Commanding rigid position setpoints against stiff physical environments leads to extreme contact chatter, force amplification, and structural fracture. The controller must regulate dynamic impedance rather than rigid kinematics.
2. **Mathematical Formulation:** Rather than enforcing a rigid coordinate, the microcontroller regulates the dynamic relationship between external interaction forces $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}$ and kinematic displacement errors $\mathbf{e}(t) = \mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{x}_d(t)$ [@hogan1985impedance]:
   $$\mathbf{M}_d (\ddot{\mathbf{x}} - \ddot{\mathbf{x}}_d) + \mathbf{D}_d (\dot{\mathbf{x}} - \dot{\mathbf{x}}_d) + \mathbf{K}_d (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_d) = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}$$

   To maintain numerical stability without external force-torque sensors, the microcontroller implements Cartesian Stiffness Control at $1000\text{ Hz}$ using the Jacobian transpose $\mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{q}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 6}$ to project Cartesian restoring forces into joint torque space ($\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{J}^T \mathbf{F}$):
   $$\boldsymbol{\tau}^* = \mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{q}) \left[ \mathbf{K}_d (\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{D}_d (\dot{\mathbf{x}}_d - \dot{\mathbf{x}}) \right] + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})$$

3. **Variable and Intuition Breakdown:**
   - $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}_d \in \mathbb{R}^6$ are measured and desired Cartesian poses (translational position in $\text{m}$ and orientation in $\text{rad}$).
   - $\mathbf{M}_d \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 6}$ is the virtual inertia matrix ($\text{kg}$ and $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$).
   - $\mathbf{D}_d \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 6}$ is the virtual damping matrix ($\text{N}\cdot\text{s/m}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$).
   - $\mathbf{K}_d \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 6}$ is the virtual stiffness matrix ($\text{N/m}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$).
   - $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ is the external contact wrench (forces in $\text{N}$ and torques in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$).
   - $\mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{q}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 6}$ is the geometric Jacobian transpose, mapping Cartesian restoring forces directly to joint torques without matrix inversion, remaining completely immune to kinematic singularities ($\det(\mathbf{J}) = 0$).
   - $\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q}) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the analytical gravity compensation torque vector ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$).

4. **Concrete Numerical Walkthrough:**
   A 2-link planar arm with end-effector target $\mathbf{x}_d = [0.60, 0.20]^T\text{ m}$ is displaced by contact to $\mathbf{x} = [0.58, 0.20]^T\text{ m}$ ($\Delta x = 0.02\text{ m} = 20\text{ mm}$). With stiffness $K_x = 500.0\text{ N/m}$, damping $D_x = 50.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}$, and zero velocity error, the virtual Cartesian restoring force is $F_x = 500.0 \times 0.02 = 10.0\text{ N}$. Given current Jacobian transpose column $\mathbf{J}_x^T(\mathbf{q}) = [-0.30, -0.15]^T\text{ m}$, the restoring joint torques compute instantly as $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{restoring}} = [-0.30, -0.15]^T \times 10.0 = [-3.00, -1.50]^T\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ plus gravity compensation.

When impedance parameters vary dynamically during contact transitions, discrete-time integration can inadvertently inject energy, causing limit cycles or contact chatter. The microcontroller guards against instability using Passivity Observers and Energy Tanks [@ferraguti2013energy]. Treating the controller as a virtual energy reservoir, the enforcer monitors power exchange ($P(t) = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}^T \dot{\mathbf{x}}$) and updates the energy tank state:

$$E_{\text{tank}}[k] = E_{\text{tank}}[k-1] + \Delta t \left( \sigma[k] P_{\text{dissipated}}[k] - P_{\text{injected}}[k] \right)$$

If the tank depletes ($E_{\text{tank}} \le E_{\text{min}}$), virtual stiffness is capped and physical damping is injected, guaranteeing that the closed-loop system remains strictly passive ($\int_0^t P(\tau) d\tau \ge -E_{\text{tank}}(0)$).

### Motor Field-Oriented Control and Thermal Safeguards

At the physical boundary where digital control setpoints become analog electromagnetic forces, the microcontroller commands brushless permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs) using Field-Oriented Control (FOC) executing at $20\text{ kHz}$ in hardware timer peripherals.

#### The Physical Analogy: The Synchronous Magnetic Carousel {.unnumbered}

In physical PMSM motors, current flows through three stator coils separated by $120^\circ$ electrical phase angles. Trying to regulate rapidly oscillating three-phase sinusoidal AC currents from a stationary frame is like trying to paint a moving horse on a spinning carousel: high rotor speeds induce phase lag and gain attenuation. 

Field-Oriented Control resolves this by mathematically stepping onto the rotating rotor carousel:

1. **Clarke Transformation:** Maps three-phase stator currents ($i_a, i_b, i_c$) onto a two-phase stationary orthogonal reference frame ($\alpha, \beta$). Leveraging Kirchhoff's current law in isolated neutral star windings ($i_a + i_b + i_c = 0 \implies i_c = -i_a - i_b$), the microcontroller computes this using two current shunt ADC readings:
   $$\begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_a \\ i_b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} i_a \\ \frac{i_a + 2 i_b}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix}$$

2. **Park Transformation:** Projects the stationary currents ($i_\alpha, i_\beta$) onto the rotating rotor reference frame ($d, q$) using the electrical rotor angle $\theta_e$ measured by optical or magnetic encoders:
   $$\begin{bmatrix} i_d \\ i_q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_e & \sin\theta_e \\ -\sin\theta_e & \cos\theta_e \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix}$$

In this rotating reference frame, the Direct Axis Current ($i_d$) controls rotor magnetic flux alignment (regulated to $i_d^* = 0$ for surface-mount permanent magnet motors to maximize electrical efficiency), while the Quadrature Axis Current ($i_q$) produces pure electromagnetic torque in direct linear proportion to the motor torque constant $K_t$:
$$\tau_{\text{motor}} = \frac{3}{2} P \cdot \lambda_{\text{pm}} \cdot i_q = K_t \cdot i_q$$
where $P$ is the number of magnetic pole pairs and $\lambda_{\text{pm}}$ ($\text{Wb}$) is the rotor permanent magnet flux linkage.

*Concrete Numerical Walkthrough:* A 4-pole-pair PMSM with torque constant $K_t = 0.25\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/A}$ measures phase currents $i_a = +10.00\text{ A}$ and $i_b = -5.00\text{ A}$ (implying $i_c = -5.00\text{ A}$) at rotor electrical angle $\theta_e = 30.0^\circ$ ($\cos 30^\circ \approx 0.866, \sin 30^\circ = 0.500$).

- Clarke transform: $i_\alpha = 10.00\text{ A}$, $i_\beta = \frac{10.00 + 2(-5.00)}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{0.00}{\sqrt{3}} = 0.00\text{ A}$.

- Park transform:
  $$i_d = \cos(30^\circ)(10.00) + \sin(30^\circ)(0.00) = 0.866 \times 10.00 = +8.66\text{ A}$$
  $$i_q = -\sin(30^\circ)(10.00) + \cos(30^\circ)(0.00) = -0.500 \times 10.00 = -5.00\text{ A}$$

- Electromagnetic torque: $\tau_{\text{motor}} = 0.25\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/A} \times (-5.00\text{ A}) = -1.25\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

The FOC current loop then adjusts inverter PWM duty cycles to drive $i_d \to 0$ and track the desired torque command $i_q^* = \tau_{\text{safe}} / K_t$.

The resulting voltage setpoints $(v_d^*, v_q^*)$ are converted into three-phase pulse-width modulation duty cycles using Space-Vector PWM (SVPWM), driving the gate voltages of isolated MOSFET/IGBT H-bridge inverters at $20\text{ kHz}$ with center-aligned ADC sampling.

To protect motor windings from thermal damage during sustained high-torque operations, the firmware executes a real-time discrete thermal accumulator:

$$T_{\text{stator}}[k] = T_{\text{stator}}[k-1] + \frac{\Delta t}{C_{\text{th}}} \left( I_{\text{phase}}^2[k] R_{\text{stator}} - \frac{T_{\text{stator}}[k-1] - T_{\text{amb}}}{R_{\text{th}}} \right)$$

where $\Delta t = 0.001\text{ s}$ ($1.0\text{ ms}$ tick), $C_{\text{th}} = 60.0\text{ J/}^\circ\text{C}$, $R_{\text{th}} = 2.00^\circ\text{C/W}$, and $R_{\text{stator}} = 0.25\,\Omega$. When estimated stator temperature exceeds the warning threshold ($T_{\text{stator}} > 85^\circ\text{C}$), the microcontroller initiates linear torque derating, preventing enamel insulation breakdown at $155^\circ\text{C}$ (NEMA Class F).

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Ideal Instantaneous Torque Generation vs. Inductive Back-EMF Collapse"}
* **The Common Assumption:** In simulation and high-level control design, motor torque $\tau$ is treated as an instantaneous algebraic function of commanded control input ($\tau = K_t i_q$), allowing the safety filter to assume commanded torque steps are realized immediately at the motor shaft.
* **The Physical Reality:** Physical motor windings have non-zero electrical inductance $L_{\text{stator}}$ and resistance $R_{\text{stator}}$, governing current dynamics by the differential equation $\frac{di_q}{dt} = \frac{v_q - R i_q - K_e \omega_m}{L}$. At high rotational speeds ($\omega_m$), the motor generates substantial back-electromotive force ($e_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega_m$) that directly opposes the inverter DC bus voltage. When the safety enforcer demands rapid counter-torque to arrest high-speed motion, the available voltage headroom $\Delta V = V_{\text{bus}} - K_e \omega_m$ collapses, capping the current slew rate $\frac{di_q}{dt}$. As a consequence, actual braking torque lags the commanded safety envelope, resulting in unmodeled stopping overshoot and physical impact.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Bare-metal safety filters enforcing dynamic stopping bounds must incorporate electro-mechanical actuator models, constraining commanded torque derivative rates to the voltage-dependent physical slew limit ($\frac{d\tau}{dt} \le K_t \frac{V_{\text{bus}} - K_e \omega_m - R i_q}{L}$) and verifying that deceleration envelopes are achievable under instantaneous back-EMF conditions.
:::

### Autopsy: The Late Commanded Deceleration

The consequences of hosting safety checks in user-space software on a general-purpose operating system are documented in the forensic autopsy of a 6-DoF industrial articulated manipulator (@fig-enforcement-platform).

::: {.callout-autopsy title="The Late Commanded Deceleration"}
* **System:** 6-DoF articulated material-handling manipulator operating at $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ in a palletizing workcell.
* **Incident:** Host Linux application processor experienced a $140\text{ ms}$ dirty page writeback memory compaction pause while approaching an obstacle at $d_{\text{clearance}} = 0.280\text{ m}$.
* **Telemetry Snapshot:** At $T-0.140\text{ s}$, ToF sensor reported $d_{\text{clearance}} = 0.280\text{ m}$; at $T-0.125\text{ s}$, kernel suspended user-space safety thread; arm coasted $0.252\text{ m}$ unguided; at $T-0.010\text{ s}$, software resumed with $0.028\text{ m}$ clearance; at $T+0.000\text{ s}$, arm struck fixture at $0.92\text{ m/s}$ ($3.4\text{ kN}$ dynamic impact).
* **Root Cause:** Arm coasted unguided for $0.252\text{ m}$ during the OS pause; when software resumed, remaining clearance was only $0.028\text{ m}$, rendering safe kinematic braking ($d_{\text{brake}} = 0.081\text{ m}$) physically impossible.
* **Architectural Flaw:** Co-locating safety monitoring in user-space software without an independent, bare-metal microcontroller holding exclusive hardware authority.
* **Provenance:** Industrial workcell failure report and flight-recorder telemetry reconstructed for systems instruction.
:::

![A 6-DoF articulated manipulator arm in the testbed, highlighting the specific harmonic drive wrist joint that fractured during the collision incident.](figures/fig08_manipulator_arm_cropped.jpg){#fig-enforcement-platform width=100%}

In this industrial workcell incident, the 6-DoF articulated manipulator was executing high-speed palletizing maneuvers at $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$. Safety monitoring and trajectory generation were co-located in a user-space process executing under standard Linux on an x86-64 host computer.

At timestamp $T - 0.140\text{ s}$, an optical time-of-flight sensor detected an unexpected fixture protrusion at a distance of $d_{\text{clearance}} = 0.280\text{ m}$. However, at that exact millisecond, the Linux kernel initiated a background memory compaction cycle to service a multi-gigabyte dirty page writeback. The user-space planning and safety process was preempted and suspended for $140\text{ ms}$.

Because the motor inverters were governed by unmanaged user-space setpoints, the actuators held the last commanded velocity. The arm coasted forward unguided:

$$d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{pause}} = 1.8\text{ m/s} \times 0.140\text{ s} = 0.252\text{ m}$$

When the Linux kernel finally resumed the safety process at $T - 0.010\text{ s}$, the remaining physical clearance had collapsed to:

$$d_{\text{remaining}} = 0.280\text{ m} - 0.252\text{ m} = 0.028\text{ m} = 2.8\text{ cm}$$

The safety software immediately commanded maximum emergency braking deceleration ($a_{\text{max}} = 20.0\text{ m/s}^2$). However, the quadratic braking distance required to arrest moving mass from $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ was:

$$d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}} = \frac{1.8^2}{2 \times 20.0} = \frac{3.24}{40.0} = 0.081\text{ m} = 8.1\text{ cm}$$

Because the required stopping distance ($8.1\text{ cm}$) exceeded the remaining physical clearance ($2.8\text{ cm}$), the collision was physically unavoidable. The manipulator struck the solid steel fixture plate at an impact velocity of $v_{\text{impact}} \approx 0.92\text{ m/s}$, generating a dynamic shock load of $F_{\text{impact}} \approx 3.4\text{ kN}$. The shock load fractured the precision flexspline teeth of the Joint 4 harmonic drive speed reducer, bent the mounting flange, and damaged internal motor bearings, incurring a $7,200\text{ USD}$ overhaul cost. The flight-recorder telemetry ledger is detailed in @tbl-telemetry-ch09.

| Timestamp | Subsystem & Substrate | Recorded State / Telemetry Event | Physical Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **$T - 0.140\text{ s}$** | Optical ToF Sensor | Detects obstacle intrusion at $d_{\text{clearance}} = 0.280\text{ m}$. | Range data dispatched to Linux MPU driver. |
| **$T - 0.125\text{ s}$** | Linux MPU Kernel | Dirty page writeback triggers memory compaction; user-space planning thread suspended. | $140\text{ ms}$ perception-planning blackout begins. |
| **$T - 0.040\text{ s}$** | Arm Actuators / Linkage | Arm continues coasting forward at $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ along un-cancelled trajectory chunk. | Reaction displacement consumes $0.252\text{ m}$ of clearance. |
| **$T - 0.010\text{ s}$** | Linux MPU / Planning Thread | Planning thread resumes; emits emergency stop command to motor drivers. | Remaining clearance is only $0.028\text{ m}$ ($2.8\text{ cm}$). |
| **$T + 0.000\text{ s}$** | Manipulator Wrist / Fixture | Arm strikes steel fixture plate at $0.92\text{ m/s}$ ($3.4\text{ kN}$ dynamic impact). | Harmonic drive flexspline fractures ($7,200\text{ USD}$ overhaul). |

: Flight-Recorder Telemetry Ledger: The Late Commanded Deceleration Incident. Tracing non-deterministic OS latency tails to mechanical gearbox fracture. {#tbl-telemetry-ch09}

### Cross-Disciplinary Autopsy Reflections

The post-incident investigation brought together the three engineering perspectives to reconstruct why the failure occurred:

- **Maya (CS/ML):** *"Our reinforcement learning policy had reached zero collision rate in training and possessed high confidence. But because the safety monitor ran in Python on the same Linux host, the model was completely blinded during the kernel writeback pause. We must never treat software assertions as physical safety guarantees."*
- **Carlos (ECE/Embedded):** *"The fatal flaw was architectural: allowing an OS-managed thread to control motor registers directly without an independent hardware watchdog. In our refactored architecture, candidate trajectories are guarded by a $50\text{ ms}$ intent lease in static SRAM. When the OS paused for $140\text{ ms}$, the microcontroller's $1000\text{ Hz}$ timer ISR would have expired the lease at $T-0.075\text{ s}$ and executed a Category 1 dynamic stop with $0.18\text{ m}$ of clearance to spare."*
- **Alex (MechE/Robotics):** *"The $3.4\text{ kN}$ impact load easily sheared the cup flexspline teeth rated for $180\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Moving mass cannot be commanded to stop without respecting $d_{\text{stop}} = v \tau + v^2/2a_{\text{max}}$. By embedding dynamic stopping envelopes into the bare-metal microcontroller, we guarantee that velocity is throttled before clearance falls below the braking threshold."*


## Safety Fallback Escalation Hierarchy

To establish a defensible physical safety boundary, the execution subsystem structures emergency responses into a certified functional safety hierarchy aligned with IEC 60204-1, IEC 61800-5-2, and ISO 13849-1 (@fig-fallback-hierarchy).

![**IEC 60204-1 Emergency Fallback Hierarchy and Hardware STO.** Multi-tier safety escalation: Category 2 (Closed-loop trajectory freeze) to Category 1 (Controlled SS1 dynamic deceleration) to Category 0 (Hardware Safe Torque Off / STO via physical optocouplers cutting gate drive power in $< 5\,\mu\text{s}$).](figures/fig08_fallback_hierarchy.svg){#fig-fallback-hierarchy width=100%}

### The Physical Analogy: The Tiered Circuit Breaker and Airbag System

To understand why multi-tier fallback is necessary, consider the mental model of a **Tiered Electrical Circuit Breaker and Vehicle Safety System**. In high-power industrial electrical distribution, electrical faults are not handled by a single crude switch. A minor, transient overload trips a soft thermal relay (allowing momentary motor inrush currents while protecting cables over minutes); a rapid, high-current surge trips an electromagnetic circuit breaker (clearing the branch in cycles); and a catastrophic arc-flash short circuit triggers a solid-state pyrotechnic disconnect fuse in microseconds.

Similarly, an embodied robot must not treat every minor timing jitter with the same extreme measure as a hardware short circuit. Cutting power instantly to an arm lifting a payload causes gravity to pull the arm down in an uncontrolled collapse. Conversely, waiting for software to gracefully stop during a gate driver short-circuit causes silicon fire. The system requires a certified, graduated escalation ladder.

### Functional Safety Escalation Hierarchy

Emergency stops are partitioned into three distinct operational tiers based on severity and hardware isolation:

1. **Category 2 Stop (Controlled Stop with Power Maintained):** Actuators remain energized while the microcontroller commands a controlled deceleration along the nominal trajectory or holds position via Cartesian impedance control. This tier is applied during transient intent lease renewals, minor boundary proximity, or recoverable human pause commands.
2. **Category 1 Stop (Controlled Stop with Dynamic Braking / Safe Stop 1, SS1):** The microcontroller actively applies maximum certified counter-electromotive braking deceleration ($a_{\text{max}}$) to bring all moving joints to a complete stop, after which power to the motor inverters is disconnected. This tier is triggered when an intent lease expires without renewal, when tracking error diverges, or when an obstacle enters the dynamic stopping envelope.
3. **Category 0 Stop (Safe Torque Off / STO):** Immediate, uncoordinated removal of electrical power from motor gate drivers via dedicated physical optocoupler interlocks in $< 5\,\mu\text{s}$. By de-energizing the optocoupler input, the gate-driver bias supply is physically grounded, dropping the gate-source voltage $V_{GS}$ below threshold ($V_{th}$). The inverter bridge MOSFETs are forced into high-impedance cutoff mode, electrically disconnecting stator coils regardless of microcontroller software state or processor freeze. Category 0 is hardwired directly to emergency e-stop buttons, hardware watchdog trip circuits, DC-link overvoltage monitors, and gate driver shoot-through protectors.

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Category 0 Safe Torque Off as a Universal Fail-Safe"}
* **The Common Assumption:** Triggering a Category 0 Safe Torque Off (cutting power to all motor inverters immediately via hardware interlocks) is always the safest emergency response during any unexpected control anomaly or boundary breach.
* **The Physical Reality:** Category 0 STO instantly eliminates active motor torque ($i_q = 0$), leaving the physical plant to decelerate solely under passive joint friction, dynamic gravity torques, and uncoordinated mechanical brakes. For a vertical articulated manipulator holding a heavy payload, triggering STO without holding brakes causes the arm to collapse downward under gravitational acceleration ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$), crashing into workcell equipment. For a high-speed mobile robot or vehicle, triggering STO removes active regenerative counter-braking and steering stabilization, transforming a controlled stop into an uncontrolled skid.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Emergency shutdown architectures must implement a certified tiered fallback hierarchy: Category 1 (Safe Stop 1, SS1) controlled dynamic braking under active power must be the default response for operational and kinematic boundary faults, reserving Category 0 STO strictly for catastrophic hardware failures (e.g., short circuits, gate driver shoot-through, or brownouts) where active inverter control is physically compromised.
:::

| **Execution Latency** | `loop.max_exec_us` | $\text{WCET} \le 175.0\,\mu\text{s}$ | $17.5\%$ CPU load margin |
| **Heap Allocation** | `mem.heap_bytes` | $0\text{ Bytes}$ (`malloc = 0`) | Pre-allocated static DTCM SRAM only |
| **Barrier Convergence** | `cbf.gamma_gain` | $\gamma = 15.0\text{ s}^{-1}$ | Class-$\mathcal{K}$ boundary decay rate |

## Systems Stress-Tests: Architectural Food for Thought

Evaluating the real-time reflex and safety enforcement tier requires navigating difficult trade-offs where control barrier theory, microsecond embedded execution, and high-power inverter dynamics intersect. The following four architectural stress-tests examine critical edge cases across bare-metal safety enforcement:

#### Stress-Test 1: The Relative-Degree Deadlock and Actuator Saturation Dilemma {.unnumbered}

An autonomous forklift carrying a $1200\text{ kg}$ pallet approaches a warehouse wall at $v = 3.5\text{ m/s}$. The safety microcontroller solves a 1 kHz Minimal-Intervention CBF-QP enforcing an obstacle clearance barrier $h(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{wall}}\|^2 - r_{\text{safe}}^2 \ge 0$.

Because position has relative degree 2 with respect to drive motor torque, the CBF inequality constrains instantaneous braking acceleration. At distance $d = 1.2\text{ m}$, the QP solver finds an instantaneous torque command that satisfies $\dot{h} \ge -\gamma h$ at $t_k$. However, this state lies outside the viability kernel: at $t_{k+1}$, satisfying the barrier requires a deceleration of $a_{\text{req}} = 8.5\text{ m/s}^2$, but tire-ground Coulomb friction limits maximum braking to $a_{\text{friction}} = \mu g = 0.6 \times 9.81 = 5.88\text{ m/s}^2$. The QP solver becomes primal infeasible ($\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}} = \emptyset$) inside the 1 ms ISR.

*When an active-set QP solver encounters mathematical infeasibility due to actuator saturation, what deterministic fallback command must execute within the remaining $175\,\mu\text{s}$ window? How must systems engineers design High-Order Control Barrier Functions (HOCBFs) to ensure that the admissible set $\mathcal{C}$ accounts for state-dependent friction limits before high-speed trajectories are authorized?*

#### Stress-Test 2: The Zero-Allocation Active-Set Iteration Bound vs. Primal Divergence {.unnumbered}

An 8-DoF collaborative humanoid arm operates with 14 active Control Barrier Functions (joint limits, self-collision spheres, workspace boundaries, and thermal barriers). The safety filter runs on an ARM Cortex-M7 with a strict execution budget of $\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$ at $1000\text{ Hz}$.

During a fast multi-link reaching motion, 6 barrier constraints activate simultaneously. The active-set solver performs iterative Givens rotations in static DTCM SRAM (`malloc = 0`). Due to near-parallel constraint hyperplanes (ill-conditioned active set), the solver requires 18 active-set iterations to converge, consuming $240\,\mu\text{s}$ and overrunning the timer ISR deadline. If firmware enforces a hard iteration ceiling ($N_{\text{iter}} \le 10$), the solver terminates with a suboptimal, non-invariant control command that violates the self-collision boundary.

*How should systems architects structure barrier hierarchies and constraint pruning (e.g., evaluating only the $K$-nearest geometric barriers based on spatial distance) to guarantee that active-set factorizations converge within a fixed, deterministic clock-cycle bound across all operational configurations?*

#### Stress-Test 3: The Category 1 Dynamic Braking vs. Inverter DC-Bus Overvoltage Spikes {.unnumbered}

A high-speed pick-and-place delta robot moving a $15\text{ kg}$ payload at $v = 4.0\text{ m/s}$ experiences an intent lease expiration fault. The safety MCU triggers a Category 1 Safe Stop 1 (SS1), commanding maximum counter-electromotive braking torque ($\tau = -K_t i_q$) to arrest motion in $45\text{ ms}$.

As the motor phases generate counter-torque, mechanical kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 120\text{ J}$) is regenerated back through the inverter bridge into the $48\text{ V}$ DC bus capacitor bank. The regenerated current surges to $I_{\text{regen}} = 55\text{ A}$, causing the DC bus voltage to spike from $48\text{ V}$ to $72\text{ V}$ in $8\text{ ms}$ ($\Delta V = \frac{I \Delta t}{C}$). This overvoltage exceeds the $60\text{ V}$ breakdown rating of the inverter MOSFETs, triggering the hardware overvoltage protection circuit to fire an immediate Category 0 Safe Torque Off (STO). With the inverter bridge floating ($0\text{ Nm}$ torque), the robot coasts un-braked at $4.0\text{ m/s}$ into the conveyor frame.

*How must real-time safety enforcers co-design dynamic braking deceleration profiles ($a_{\text{brake}}$) with power electronics constraints (DC bus capacitance, brake chopper resistors, and regenerative current absorption) to prevent emergency stops from triggering secondary electrical hardware trips?*

#### Stress-Test 4: The Tactile Impedance Relaxation vs. Hard Position Enclosure {.unnumbered}

A collaborative robot arm is equipped with joint torque sensors executing Cartesian impedance control ($M \ddot{\mathbf{x}} + D \dot{\mathbf{x}} + K (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}}) = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}$) to safely co-exist with human operators. A hard Control Barrier Function simultaneously enforces a virtual safety fence ($x_{\text{tcp}} \le x_{\text{wall}}$).

A human worker inadvertently leans against the robot arm, applying an external contact force of $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = 80\text{ N}$ toward the virtual wall. The impedance controller yields compliantly to protect the human from bruising, deflecting the end-effector toward the boundary. As the position approaches the safety fence, the CBF-QP overrides the compliance controller, commanding maximum counter-torque ($K_{\text{stiff}} \to \infty$) to prevent the barrier breach. This instantaneous stiffness step exerts a rigid $450\text{ N}$ reactionary force against the human operator's arm, causing soft-tissue injury.

*How should systems engineers unify compliant physical human-robot interaction with inviolable geometric barrier certificates? Can Control Barrier Functions natively modulate impedance stiffness and damping parameters rather than commanding rigid kinematic projections when interacting with compliant biological bodies?*


## Master Capstone Synthesis of Part II

With the completion of the real-time safety enforcement layer, we conclude Part II's systematic journey through the Five Cognitive Organs of Physical AI.

Across Chapters 5 through 9, we have constructed the complete, closed-loop cyber-physical pipeline from first principles:

$$W_t \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 5}]{\text{Perceive}} O_t \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 6}]{\text{Remember}} S_t \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 7}]{\text{Reason}} I_t (\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}) \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 8}]{\text{Plan}} \tau_t (p_t) \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 9}]{\text{Execute}} u_t^* \xrightarrow{\text{Actuation}} W_{t+1}$$

1. **Perception (@sec-perception):** Transduced raw photon fluxes into compact 3D metric affordance tokens in $SE(3)$ using zero-copy DMA pipelines and self-supervised ViT spatial encoders.
2. **Memory (@sec-state):** Sustained continuous spatial belief across visual occlusions through Lie algebra coordinate frame trees, JEPAs, and expanding uncertainty envelopes.
3. **Intent (@sec-intent):** Grounded open-world natural language instructions through System 2 VLAs, emitting time-bounded Expiring Intent Leases ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}$) screened by kinematic reachability.
4. **Planning (@sec-planning):** Amortized neural inference latency via System 1.5 Action Chunking ($H=16$), enforcing $\mathcal{C}^2$ quintic polynomial spline continuity to eliminate gearbox jerk.
5. **Execution (@sec-enforcement):** Enforced physical forward invariance on bare-metal microcontroller silicon at $1000\text{ Hz}$ in zero-allocation SRAM (`malloc = 0`) using Minimal-Intervention CBF-QPs and $20\text{ kHz}$ Field-Oriented Control.

### The Cyber-Physical Dataflow Contracts

The five cognitive organs operate across vast disparities in bandwidth and privilege, synchronized through formal engineering contracts:

- **Rate Transitions:** Multi-rate synchronization decouples slow, high-capacity neural inference from fast, low-latency physical control:
  $$\begin{aligned}
  30\text{ Hz (Perception)} &\longrightarrow 100\text{ Hz (Memory)} \longrightarrow 5\text{ Hz (Intent)} \\
  &\longrightarrow 20\text{ Hz (Planning)} \longrightarrow 1000\text{ Hz (Safety Enforcer)} \longrightarrow 20\text{ kHz (Motor FOC)}
  \end{aligned}$$

- **Privilege and Trust Boundaries:** Generative neural policies execute in untrusted user space under standard operating systems, producing candidate trajectories governed by expiring intent leases ($\tau_{\text{lease}} \le 100\text{ ms}$). Exclusive hardware actuation authority is held by bare-metal microcontrollers operating in zero-allocation SRAM (`malloc = 0`).
- **Interface Lineage:** The cyber-physical pipeline is governed by five formal interfaces: Spatial Perception (Tokenization and Spatial Density) $\to$ Temporal Memory (Belief Purity and Latency) $\to$ Semantic Intent (Task Decomposition and Reachability) $\to$ Trajectory Planning (Chunk Horizons and $\mathcal{C}^2$ Jerk Bounding) $\to$ Real-Time Enforcement (Microsecond CBF-QP Projection and IEC 60204-1 Emergency Hierarchy).
